\title{TimeGym: Contract-Based Verification and Diagnosis\newline for Forecasting Pipelines}
\author{Diogo Seca}
\date{2026-11-05\\\small TimeGym 1.1.0; working manuscript: reproducible controlled studies}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Forecast accuracy alone does not distinguish an implementation fault from
a model limitation or future noise. TimeGym makes that distinction
explicit through forecast contracts, conditional references, declared
behavioral relations, and reproducible repair rechecks. The Python package
supports point forecasts, marginal quantiles, and joint trajectory samples
over five core Gaussian families and univariate and multivariate composed
and financial stresses, including jumps, conditional volatility, and hidden regimes.
Reference capabilities and approximation status are explicit. References
condition on observed history and generator parameters; ordinary forecasters receive only the
history and forecast indices. Two controlled studies evaluate selected output
corruptions and four internal regressions in a fitted recursive lag-Ridge
pipeline across six conditions. All four internal regressions preserve the
output contract. Scalar translation detects one, target-specific
translation detects two, and an independent implementation comparator
detects all selected regressions. A specified repair restores algorithm
agreement yet worsens mean forecast loss in one random-walk-with-drift condition,
demonstrating that implementation correctness and predictive quality are
distinct objectives. For joint forecasts, coordinate permutations preserve
every empirical marginal exactly while changing trajectory dependence;
factorized negative controls and a multiple-testing study expose the
assumptions and power limits of a reference-covariance check. A separate
real-series example reproduces one known preprocessing repair. The
contribution is an executable diagnostic workflow with transparent,
paired evidence about what each check establishes. The studies support
those specified properties and selected faults; they do not estimate
coverage of naturally occurring forecasting defects.
\end{abstract}

\paragraph{Keywords.} Time series; forecasting; software testing; conditional
references; probabilistic verification; mutation testing; reproducibility.

\caption{\textbf{A forecasting test suite at a glance.} The quick-start recursive
lag-Ridge pipeline (24 lags, ridge penalty 1, standardized lag inputs) is fitted
afresh to six configurations from five families,
each at three fixed seeds (11, 22, 33). The two random-walk rows share the same
innovations within each seed: one has zero drift and the other adds 0.03 per
step. A driftless walk can still appear to trend by chance; unlike white
noise in levels, both walks accumulate shocks. Gray dots show observations;
blue crosses are unconnected point
forecasts; thin gray curves are the privileged conditional means. Dashed
vertical lines mark the forecast origin. Every model is fitted on 300 values
and predicts 100 steps; for print readability, panels show the final 72
context values and first 48 forecasts. Value scales vary by panel.}
\label{fig:forecast-matrix}
\end{figure}

\section{Introduction}

A forecasting system is more than its fitted estimator. Indexing,
preprocessing, target construction, state handling, output conversion, and
evaluation all influence its behavior. An inaccurate forecast may result
from a software fault, a model that cannot represent the required pattern,
limited training information, or irreducible uncertainty. Conversely, a
favorable average loss does not establish that the output obeys its
declared contract.

Consider three failures. A forecast has the wrong number of future steps;
its shape violates an interface contract. A last-value predictor returns
the required shape but misses a deterministic slope; this can be an honest
capability limitation. A sample-based predictor retains the correct
distribution at every future coordinate but corrupts the pairing between
coordinates; point and marginal uncertainty scores can remain unchanged.
These failures require different evidence and different remedies.

TimeGym makes these distinctions explicit. Its intended use is to
test a forecasting pipeline before deployment and to reproduce a failure
after one. Here verification means
exercising specified runtime contracts, not formal proof of a program.
A scenario defines a
controlled data-generating process (DGP), the information exposed to the
forecaster, and the conditional references available to the evaluator.
A forecast contract defines the meaning and axes of returned values.
Diagnostics record the violated contract or the observed capability gap,
together with the case configuration and seed. Known mutations and their
repairs provide a way to test the diagnostic instrument itself.

The contribution is an executable diagnostic workflow for forecasting
tests. It connects three kinds of evidence: output contracts,
consistency with a known conditional reference, and declared relations
between transformed tasks. The implementation makes their assumptions,
outcomes, and counterexamples inspectable. Five Gaussian scenario families
provide the transparent references used in the controlled studies; additional
composed and financial mechanisms extend the software catalog. Paired
clean, faulty, and repaired runs evaluate the diagnostic instrument itself. A marginal-preserving
trajectory mutation shows that identical marginal forecasts can conceal
different joint forecasts.

This design supports a practical debugging sequence: reproduce a failing
property, inspect a candidate cause, change the implementation, and rerun
the same case and its clean controls. The report identifies the failed
property; the intervention supplies evidence about the candidate cause.
Neither a capability gap nor one successful repair identifies every
fault in a pipeline.

\subsection{Relationship to the original TimeGym proposal}

The 2021 proposal introduced synthetic challenges for debugging forecasting
pipelines~\cite{seca2021timegym}. This revision retains that practical aim
while revising its statistical specification. The original compared
forecasts with a noise-free generator component using sMAPE, a measure
whose treatment of positive and negative errors is itself
asymmetric~\cite{goodwin1999asymmetry}, and described
that component as an optimal forecast. In this revision, the reference depends
explicitly on the requested functional, loss, and information set: a
conditional mean is appropriate for squared loss, and future random
structure must be integrated out rather than treated as known. Fresh
synthetic samples do not remove adaptive selection or multiple-testing
concerns. Finally, successful synthetic tests provide evidence about the
tested mechanisms; they do not establish performance on real data. The
features and experiments described here belong to the current work and
are not attributed retrospectively to 2021.

\section{Related work and positioning}

\subsection{The oracle problem}

Testing a forecasting pipeline is an instance of the test oracle problem.
Weyuker called a program non-testable when no oracle exists or the oracle
is too costly to use, and listed the remedies that remain available: a
partial oracle, tests on simplified data with known results, and known
properties of the output~\cite{weyuker1982testing}. Davis and Weyuker
had already proposed the pseudo-oracle, an independently produced implementation of the
same specification whose outputs are compared with those of the program
under test, within a tolerance for numerical programs~\cite{davis1981pseudo}.
Guderlei and Mayer extended metamorphic relations to programs with random
output by comparing the output distributions of related executions with
hypothesis tests~\cite{guderlei2007statistical}. Oracle issues specific to
machine learning were reviewed in~\cite{seca2021review}. Table~\ref{tab:oracles}
maps the evidence used in this paper onto these oracle types. None of the
types is new; the contribution is to make each one executable for
forecasts, with its assumptions recorded.

CRADLE uses cross-implementation comparison as an oracle for
deep-learning libraries~\cite{pham2019cradle}. Tolerance-based assertions
are common in their test suites and a recurring source of flaky
tests~\cite{nejadgholi2019study,dutta2020detecting}; the explicit
\code{INCONCLUSIVE} outcome keeps a tolerance choice from being reported
as a verdict. Declared relations are properties in the sense of
property-based testing, stated beside the code and checked on generated
inputs~\cite{claessen2000quickcheck}; here the scenario generators supply
those inputs.

\subsection{Controlled tasks, conformance, and metamorphic testing}

Controlled forecasting tasks, software conformance, and metamorphic
testing provide complementary precedents (Table~\ref{tab:positioning}).
SynTSBench connects configurable temporal features to model capability,
irregularity robustness, and theoretical performance
boundaries~\cite{tan2025syntsbench}. SimpleTimeBench uses elementary
patterns and leading covariates to diagnose time-series foundation
models~\cite{ghoroghchian2026simpletimebench}; its October 2026 version is
a preprint. Synthetic challenges and known-generator references alone
therefore do not distinguish the present contribution.

FinStressTS is the closest financial precedent: it evaluates
isolated and composed synthetic mechanisms, including conditional volatility,
heavy tails, regimes, and jumps~\cite{sun2026finstressts}. Financial stress
composition alone is therefore not a novelty claim here. TimeGym emphasizes
declared forecast contracts, controlled implementation faults, and repair
rechecks. Real financial evaluation also needs target-specific protocols;
FinTSB includes market constraints and transaction costs~\cite{hu2026fintsb}.
The present synthetic tests do not establish trading performance or rank
contemporary forecasting architectures.

Dwarakanath et al. specified 19 metamorphic relations for a forecasting
application, reported eight previously unknown issues, and evaluated
mutation detection in a reference LSTM~\cite{dwarakanath2019metamorphic}.
This is a direct methodological predecessor, including evidence on actual
application defects that our selected-mutation studies do not provide.
TimeGym extends the practical testing workflow with explicit conditional
reference semantics and separate marginal and joint forecast contracts;
it does not introduce forecasting metamorphic testing.

Framework conformance and evaluation practice also matter. The sktime
\code{check\_estimator} utility runs tests appropriate to an estimator's
unified interface~\cite{sktimeConformance}. TFB standardizes evaluation
pipelines to make forecasting comparisons more consistent and
reproducible~\cite{qiu2024tfb}. TimeGym can sit beside these checks: an API
can be well formed while an application-specific transformation violates
a declared relation. We do not measure comparative detection power
against these frameworks or benchmark their forecasting models.
Production checklists for machine-learning systems are written as
assertions and scored~\cite{breck2017test}; TimeGym supplies
forecasting-specific assertions for the model evaluation stage of that
workflow~\cite{amershi2019software}.

\subsection{Statistical foundations}

Point forecasts must be
evaluated using a loss consistent with the requested
functional~\cite{gneiting2011point}: the mean is optimal under squared
error, any median under absolute error, and a quantile under the
asymmetric piecewise-linear loss~\cite{gneiting2011quantiles}.
Probabilistic forecasts are assessed by the paradigm of maximizing
sharpness subject to calibration, where calibration is a joint property of
forecasts and observations and sharpness a property of the forecasts
alone~\cite{gneiting2007probabilistic,gneiting2014probabilistic}. Proper
scoring rules address both at once~\cite{gneiting2007proper}. The CRPS
originates in the integrated quadratic score of Matheson and
Winkler~\cite{matheson1976scoring}; for an ensemble it decomposes into
reliability, resolution, and uncertainty
terms~\cite{hersbach2000decomposition}, and it can be weighted toward
tails or quantiles while remaining proper~\cite{gneiting2011comparing}.
The energy score generalizes the CRPS to multivariate quantities, and the
multivariate rank histogram checks ensemble
calibration~\cite{gneiting2008assessing}; variogram-based scores respond
to dependence misspecification~\cite{scheuerer2015variogram}. Interval
forecasts require conditional, not merely unconditional,
coverage~\cite{christoffersen1998evaluating}.
Our contribution uses these principles to specify executable tests;
it does not propose a new scoring rule.

\section{Forecasting tasks and conditional references}

\subsection{Information and estimands}

Let $Y_t\in\R^D$ denote the target vector and let the observed context be
$y_{0:L-1}$. The task requests $H$ future steps,
$Y_{L:L+H-1}$. The model-facing information consists of this context and
the forecast indices. In the implemented generators, the evaluator also
knows the fixed DGP parameters $\theta$. Its reference distribution is
\begin{equation}
 F_\theta = \mathcal{L}\!\left(Y_{L:L+H-1}
       \mid Y_{0:L-1}=y_{0:L-1},\theta\right).
\end{equation}
Future innovations are integrated out, not exposed to the forecaster.
The ordinary adapter receives neither the realized future nor the
reference. Declared change schedules are also evaluator-only information.
Deliberately privileged controls used to test the evaluator
are identified separately.

For a conditional-mean forecast, the reference at lead $h$ and target $d$ is
$m_{hd}=\E_\theta[Y_{L+h-1,d}\mid y_{0:L-1}]$, with $h=1,\ldots,H$.
Let $K=HD$, let $\Sigma_F$ be the covariance of the flattened future vector,
and let $a$ be a forecast based only on the allowed information and
independent model randomness. Conditional squared-error risk decomposes as
\begin{equation}
 \frac{1}{K}\E_\theta[\|Y-a\|_2^2\mid y_{0:L-1},a]
 = \frac{1}{K}\|m-a\|_2^2 + \frac{1}{K}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_F).
\end{equation}
Thus mean-reference MSE measures conditional excess squared-error risk
under the known DGP. It is different from realized test-set MSE, which
contains future randomness. It is also a privileged target: a learned
forecaster must infer structure and parameters from finite history.
A nonzero gap alone does not establish an implementation fault.

For level $q\in(0,1)$, the reference is instead the marginal conditional
quantile $F_{\theta,hd}^{-1}(q)$, evaluated using pinball loss. A median
forecast corresponds to absolute error. Conditional means and medians
coincide in the five core Gaussian families. They generally differ in the
asymmetric price and jump distributions; the requested functional must
remain explicit.
Marginal quantiles do not determine the joint distribution of trajectories.

\subsection{Core Gaussian scenario families}

Figure~\ref{fig:forecast-matrix} shows these mechanisms as a visual test suite.


Let $\epsilon_t\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\Omega)$, where
$\Omega=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma)R\operatorname{diag}(\sigma)$ and $R$
is a valid target-correlation matrix. Innovations are independent across
time but can be correlated across targets. Vector operations below are
componentwise, and $\phi$ is scalar.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.73\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Family & Data-generating equation and conditional mean \\
\midrule
Fixed-mean white noise & $Y_t=\mu+\epsilon_t$; $m_h=\mu$. \\[0.5em]
Linear trend + noise & $Y_t=b+ct+\epsilon_t$; $m_h=b+c(L+h-1)$. \\[0.5em]
Fixed seasonality + noise & $Y_t=\mu+A\sin(2\pi t/p)+\epsilon_t$; evaluate the same deterministic part at $t=L+h-1$. \\[0.5em]
Stationary AR(1) & $Y_t=\mu+\phi(Y_{t-1}-\mu)+\epsilon_t$, $|\phi|<1$; $m_h=\mu+\phi^h(y_{L-1}-\mu)$. \\[0.5em]
Random walk (optional drift) & $Y_t=Y_{t-1}+c+\epsilon_t$; $m_h=y_{L-1}+hc$. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\paragraph{White noise, deterministic structure, and accumulated shocks.}
These are distinct processes, even when one short realization looks similar.
Fixed-mean Gaussian white noise fluctuates around $\mu$; linear trend plus
white noise fluctuates around $b+ct$; fixed seasonality plus white noise
fluctuates around a repeating sinusoid. In all three, a shock at time $t$
does not carry into later observations. A random walk instead has
$Y_t=Y_0+ct+\sum_{s=1}^{t}\epsilon_s$: shocks persist in its level. Its
centered increments $Y_t-Y_{t-1}-c$, rather than its levels, are white noise.
The parameter $c$ is the optional \emph{drift}, an expected change per step;
$c=0$ does not prevent an individual path from wandering upward or downward.
With known parameters and scalar innovation
variance $\sigma^2$, the random walk's conditional variance is $h\sigma^2$
at horizon $h$; the three deterministic-mean, fresh-noise processes retain
$\sigma^2$. Thus the difference concerns shock persistence and uncertainty,
not just a visible slope.

The AR(1) context starts from the stationary law
$Y_0\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Omega/(1-\phi^2))$; the random walk starts at
a specified deterministic intercept. For white noise, trend, and
seasonality, future covariance blocks are
$\Cov(Y_{L+h-1},Y_{L+j-1}\mid y)=\mathbf{1}_{h=j}\Omega$.
For AR(1), define the lower-triangular innovation map
$B_{hk}=\phi^{h-k}\mathbf{1}_{k\leq h}$, for $h,k=1,\ldots,H$.
The full covariance is $(BB^\top)\otimes\Omega$, using horizon-major
flattening. For a random walk, covariance block $(h,j)$ is
$\min(h,j)\Omega$. The conditional marginal quantiles are
\begin{equation}
 Q_{hd}(q)=m_{hd}+\sqrt{(\Sigma_F)_{(h,d),(h,d)}}\,\Phi^{-1}(q).
\end{equation}
Zero innovation variance gives a deterministic reference.

Reference validation compares analytic quantities with conditional
simulations and tests boundary cases such as zero noise and correlation
validity. Simulation agreement is an implementation check; it is not an
independent proof when simulator and reference share code. Algebraic
checks and explicit small cases are therefore also needed. These five
core families provide the original study conditions. The extensions below
add selected mechanisms; missingness, exogenous covariates and irregular
sampling remain outside the implemented scenario scope.

\subsection{Seasonality, process drift, and changing mechanisms}

Seasonality is recurring structure; a fixed sinusoid is not the drift term
of a random walk. Nor is a stable seasonal law automatically concept drift
when calendar phase is included in the conditioning information. We distinguish
\emph{process drift}, an expected increment, from changes in the generating
parameters or predictive relationship~\cite{gama2014drift}. The latter can
change a trend slope, seasonal amplitude, period or phase, innovation scale,
or dependence. Likewise, a GARCH variance state or a hidden Markov regime
can change under a fixed law: a state transition and a parameter change are
separate experimental interventions.

The \code{composite} scenario specifies a deterministic component
$g_t=b+ct+A\sin(2\pi t/p+\phi)$ and one residual process: fresh Gaussian
noise or an accumulated-shock process. The latter may include independent
compound-Poisson increments. Declared changes can replace mean parameters
or noise scale at an explicit index. The before/after mean uses absolute
$t$, so changing the slope need not preserve level continuity. These are
additive level constructions, not multiplicative financial price models.
The evaluator knows the change schedule; an ordinary fitted model does not.

\subsection{Financial stress mechanisms and non-Gaussian references}

Figure~\ref{fig:financial-stresses} illustrates the financial extensions.
The additional financial families isolate established stochastic mechanisms
and selected interactions. Price, log price, log return, and volatility are different
forecast targets. Both the core Gaussian families and these extensions
support multivariate targets under explicit dependence laws. The existing
\code{Scenario} and \code{Pipeline} interfaces apply to both groups.

For \code{merton\_jump\_diffusion}, let $J_i\sim\mathcal N(a,b_J^2)$,
$N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda\Delta t)$, and
$\kappa=\exp(a+b_J^2/2)-1$. Independent one-step log returns follow
\begin{equation}
 R=(\mu-\tfrac12\sigma^2-\lambda\kappa)\Delta t
   +\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z+\sum_{i=1}^{N}J_i,
 \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\end{equation}
This is the Merton construction~\cite{merton1976jumps}, using a physical
expected-price-growth convention rather than a risk-neutral pricing
calibration. Zero jump intensity reduces it to geometric Brownian motion.
The cumulant $K(u)=\log\E[e^{uR}]$ gives the conditional price mean
$S_T\exp(hK(1))$ and price covariance; exponentiating a conditional
log-price mean generally gives the wrong mean on the price scale.

For \code{garch}, Gaussian innovations follow
$r_t=\mu+\sqrt{v_t}z_t$ and
$v_{t+1}=\omega+\alpha(r_t-\mu)^2+\beta v_t$, with
$\omega>0$, $\alpha,\beta\geq0$, and $\alpha+\beta<1$; this is the GARCH
generalization~\cite{bollerslev1986garch} of Engle's ARCH
process~\cite{engle1982autoregressive}.
The next variance is reconstructed from observed returns. Each simulated
future recursively updates its own variance; replacing that recursion by
independent Gaussian draws with expected variances loses part of the joint
law. The implementation supplies log-return or log-price tasks, not price
moments obtained by an unjustified exponentiation.

For \code{markov\_switching}, a finite hidden Markov chain controls return
means, diffusion scales, and optionally jump parameters. The reference
filters $\Pr(S_T\mid y_{0:T},\theta)$ from observed returns and propagates
that distribution, following the hidden-regime principle~\cite{hamilton1989regimes}.
It never conditions on the simulator's actual terminal regime. Gaussian
emission filtering supports an exact conditional sampler under the declared
law. With jumps, the emission likelihood is a truncated Poisson mixture:
its omitted probability mass is recorded, but is not a posterior-error
bound. Those references are marked approximate.

\code{SimulationReference} retains analytical means and either analytical or
explicitly estimated covariance under its declared conditioning distribution,
and draws joint futures from an explicit sampler.
Its marginal quantiles are reproducible Monte Carlo estimates, with sample
count and seed recorded, rather than Gaussian quantiles inferred from two
moments. The covariance rank check returns \texttt{UNSUPPORTED} for
approximate conditional samplers. Shape checks and descriptive forecast
scores remain available; no exact test guarantee is attached to the
approximate hidden-regime reference.

A useful development sequence isolates mechanisms, compares matched pairs,
then adds supported interactions. Seeds, parameter regions, and compositions
must be reserved from model development; a synthetic suite can itself be
overfit. After pipeline selection, untouched real data and rolling forecast
origins provide a separate transfer assessment. The executable extension
examples and mathematical validation do not expand the Gaussian fault-study
corpus reported in Sections~\ref{sec:implementation-study} and~\ref{sec:results}.

last-value forecaster is fitted to six configurations at seeds 11, 22 and 33.
The first pair contrasts geometric Brownian motion with Merton jumps in log

regimes combined with jumps, and the combined process on the price scale.

\subsection{Joint mechanisms and dependence-aware uncertainty}
\label{sec:joint-stresses}

The same four identifiers accept $D>1$ targets. Each sampled future is an
$H\times D$ array, and covariance uses horizon-major vectorization. A sample
index identifies one complete future; fitting each target separately and
independently drawing its uncertainty generally does not reproduce that law.
Scalar location and scale parameters broadcast over targets, while vectors
specify target-specific values. The implementation separates ordinary-shock
correlation, jump-size correlation, shared jump arrivals, and shared regimes.

For additive compositions, innovation covariance is
$\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_t)R
\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_t)$. An optional shared Poisson clock
adds vector marks $\boldsymbol J\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol a,B)$, giving
increment covariance
\begin{equation}
 Q_t=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_t)R
       \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_t)
       +\lambda(B+\boldsymbol a\boldsymbol a^\top).
\end{equation}
Fresh residuals have block-diagonal time covariance. Accumulated residuals
sum $Q_t$ through the earlier of the two forecast horizons. Scheduled changes
may affect different targets differently; their future schedule remains
an evaluator information advantage.

Joint Merton returns use correlated diffusion and one shared Poisson arrival
process, with a separate correlation matrix for Gaussian log-jump marks.
The cumulant construction extends to vectors. For
$K(\boldsymbol u)=\log\E\exp(\boldsymbol u^\top\boldsymbol R)$ and coordinate
vectors $\boldsymbol e_i$, conditional price covariance is
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Cov}(S_{T+h,i},S_{T+k,j}\mid\mathcal I_T)
 =m_{h,i}m_{k,j}\left[
 \exp\!\left(\min(h,k)
 \{K(\boldsymbol e_i+\boldsymbol e_j)-K(\boldsymbol e_i)
 -K(\boldsymbol e_j)\}\right)-1\right].
\end{equation}
Here $K$ includes one observation step and $m_{h,i}$ is the conditional price
mean. Zero ordinary-shock correlation does not remove dependence from a
shared jump clock. The declared construction has common jump arrivals;
it does not add an unspecified independent jump process for each target.

The GARCH extension is constant-conditional-correlation GARCH
(CCC-GARCH)~\cite{bollerslev1990ccc}:
$\boldsymbol\epsilon_t=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\boldsymbol v_t})
\boldsymbol z_t$, with $\boldsymbol z_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R)$ and one
GARCH(1,1) recursion per target. Conditional simulation updates all variance
states along each future trajectory. Means and marginal variances are
analytical; cross-time return covariances vanish. However, future same-time
cross-series covariance contains
\begin{equation}
 R_{ij}\,\E[\sqrt{v_{T+h,i}v_{T+h,j}}\mid\mathcal I_T],
\end{equation}
which is generally not $R_{ij}\sqrt{\E[v_{T+h,i}]\E[v_{T+h,j}]}$.
An independent Monte Carlo ensemble estimates the expected conditional
covariance, rescaled to the analytical diagonal to preserve both known
marginal variances and positive semidefiniteness. The sample count and seed
are recorded; the default count is 16,384. First-step, zero-correlation,
and fully deterministic-variance cases use analytical covariance.
Log-level covariance accumulates the return blocks.

These numerical moments are labeled
\code{analytic\_mean\_monte\_carlo\_covariance}; the conditional sampler
remains exact under the declared law. Covariance rank calibration holds the
estimated target matrix fixed, using independent forecast and null ensembles.
Conditional on that fixed target, the statistics remain exchangeable under
the null. This separates the validity of rank calibration from the precision
of the numerical covariance, which may affect diagnostic power. The check
still cannot detect every form of higher-order dependence.

Joint Markov scenarios share one hidden chain. Regime parameters may be
$K\times D$ arrays, and within-regime correlation may differ by state. The
forward filter uses the complete observed return vector, never the simulated
state. Analytical recursions propagate the filtered distribution and all
cross-target/cross-horizon moments. With shared jumps, a truncated multivariate
Gaussian mixture approximates each emission likelihood; the existing
approximate-reference diagnostic guard applies. Multivariate filtering
requires positive diffusion scales and positive-definite state correlation
matrices, while the other joint families also support singular correlations.

Figure~\ref{fig:joint-stresses} shows a targeted pairing fault: permuting one
target's entire sample trajectories preserves its marginal distributions and
within-target temporal paths, while changing dependence between targets.

A two-target Merton log-price reference supplies 768 joint six-step futures
for one fixed case from notebook 27. The right column re-pairs target 1's
complete trajectories across sample identities. The top panels show the
first 384 draws at horizon four, standardized by reference means and standard
deviations, within a fixed $\pm4.5$ display window. Blue crosses mark the
unchanged conditional means. Correlation maps and aggregate standard
deviations use all 768 draws; matrix coordinates alternate targets within
each horizon. The aggregate is the equal-weight average of
the two standardized forecast errors, not a portfolio-return estimate.

CRPS is unchanged up to floating-point roundoff. These reference ensembles
illustrate a controlled dependence fault.}

\section{Executable contracts and diagnostic reports}

\subsection{Output representation}

A forecast can contain point values of shape $(H,D)$, marginal quantiles
of shape $(H,D,Q)$ with strictly increasing levels in $(0,1)$, and sample
trajectories of shape $(S,H,D)$. Every sample index denotes one complete
joint future across both horizon and target axes. Exact shapes prevent
accidental NumPy broadcasting from silently changing the estimand.
Forecast indices and target names must match the requested values and
order. Returned values must be finite; quantiles must not cross. An unsupported
representation is recorded explicitly instead of being counted as a pass.

These contracts are stronger than accepting an arbitrary array, but do
not fully specify forecasting behavior. An explicitly displaced index or
reversed target-name list is detectable. Values shifted internally while
retaining apparently correct labels require task-specific references or
explicit invariants. The implementation supplies a bounded set of checks
rather than an exhaustive information-flow verifier.

\subsection{Outcomes and interpretation}

Each diagnostic returns a named outcome, evidence, and an explanation.
The outcomes are \code{PASS}, \code{FAIL}, \code{INCONCLUSIVE},
\code{UNSUPPORTED}, and \code{ERROR}. They distinguish a satisfied
implemented check, an observed violation, insufficient evidence, an
inapplicable check, and an execution failure. A model exception is not
silently converted into a numerical loss. Missing representations do not
count as successful verification.

Structural checks identify definite violations of the declared output
contract, and malformed outputs are not scored. Capability scores are
descriptive and return \code{INCONCLUSIVE} because the package does not
impose a universal acceptance tolerance. They can reflect statistical
estimation, a deliberately limited model class, or an implementation fault.
Coverage computed across one path's dependent horizon-target coordinates
is also descriptive; it does not establish calibration. The report
identifies the affected property and a reproducible case, not a unique
source-code cause. Suspected explanations require an intervention.

A \code{Pipeline} entry point runs the scenario suite and produces
machine-readable records. Reproducibility requires more than a seed: the
case parameters, model identification, forecast dimensions, implementation
and environment versions, diagnostic settings, and all outcomes must be
retained. Experiment artifacts record these together with the generated
results. Scope is explicit: these metadata do not make arbitrary external
training code deterministic.

\subsection{A reproducible diagnosis and repair workflow}

Table~\ref{tab:workflow} summarizes the operational sequence. A
\code{Pipeline.run} call retains the report and case predictions, so a
forecast plot and an error plot can describe the same execution without
refitting. A failed case can then be regenerated from its recorded scenario
configuration. Reproduction establishes that a property fails under those
conditions; investigating and modifying the implementation remain explicit
developer actions.

The evidence determines the next action. A horizon or index mismatch is a
direct contract violation. A covariance rejection is evidence against the
specified sampling law under the stated Monte Carlo null. A discrepancy
under a declared shift relation contradicts that relation, provided the
transformation preserves the model's intended task. A large conditional
mean gap without such a contract is a capability observation. A useful
repair recheck repeats the original case, its transformed counterpart
when applicable, and clean controls, retaining failures as well as passes.

\subsection{A reference-covariance check}

When a reference covariance, an exact conditional sampler, and at least
20 joint sample paths with $K\geq2$ are available, an optional Monte Carlo
check compares the ensemble covariance with the reference. The pilot uses
analytical covariance; Section~\ref{sec:joint-stresses} describes an
independently estimated, fixed target for general CCC-GARCH cross-moments. Let $\widehat\Sigma_X$ use the
usual $S-1$ denominator. The discrepancy is
\begin{equation}
 T(X)=\frac{\|\widehat\Sigma_X-\Sigma_F\|_F}{\|\Sigma_F\|_F}.
\end{equation}
A zero reference norm is reported as \code{UNSUPPORTED}. Draw $B$
independent calibration ensembles, each containing $S$ independent paths
from the same conditional law, and calculate
\begin{equation}
 p_{\mathrm{MC}}=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{B}
                \mathbf{1}\{T(X_b)\geq T(X)\}}{B+1}.
 \label{eq:mc}
\end{equation}
Under the null that the submitted ensemble itself consists of independent
draws from that reference law, the $B+1$ statistics are exchangeable.
The Monte Carlo rank rule therefore controls the per-check rejection
probability at the attainable discrete levels, with conservative treatment
of ties~\cite{hope1968montecarlo}.
The pilot uses $B=99$ and rejects when $p_{\mathrm{MC}}\leq0.05$.
Insufficient rank resolution for the requested level is
\code{INCONCLUSIVE}. No adjustment across multiple cases is automatic.

This is a reference-sampling consistency check, not a test of all forms of
forecast calibration. Variance errors as well as dependence errors can
trigger it. Failure to reject does not establish equality of covariance
or distributions. In particular, an ensemble generated by deterministic
quadrature, dependent Monte Carlo, or a learned parameter estimate does
not satisfy the stated null merely because it is a useful forecast.
The Gaussian reference is fully specified in this pilot, which makes
null simulation feasible but limits direct application to real data.

% END VECTOR FIGURE paper-dependence
\caption{\textbf{A marginally identical forecast can have different joint dependence.}
Top: the first predefined pilot case (seed 10000), with 128 exact-reference
samples and their fully coordinate-permuted counterparts. The first-horizon
target-pair clouds change, while the displayed marginal empirical CDFs
coincide; all 16 horizon--target marginal sample sets are exactly unchanged.
Bottom: mutated-minus-clean score means and paired 95\% t intervals over
64 independent cases, at the protocol's fixed permutation strengths. Points
are unconnected and score panels use different scales. CRPS changes are
floating-point roundoff; joint-score changes expose this selected dependence
alteration. Intervals are exploratory and unadjusted. The illustration does
not imply that shuffling every law is a fault: factorized white noise is a
negative control in the supplement.}
\label{fig:dependence}
\end{figure}


Figure~\ref{fig:dependence} makes the marginal--joint distinction visible
before its algebraic formulation. All reported scores are losses, so lower is better. Point results include
realized MSE and distance from the conditional mean. Marginal quantiles
use pinball loss. Ensemble CRPS is averaged over individual horizon-target
coordinates. For flattened ensemble paths $x^{(s)}\in\R^K$ and observation
$y$, the empirical energy score is
\begin{equation}
 \widehat{\mathrm{ES}} = \frac1S\sum_s\|x^{(s)}-y\|_2
 -\frac{1}{2S^2}\sum_{s,r}\|x^{(s)}-x^{(r)}\|_2.
\end{equation}
The implementation includes diagonal sample pairs and scores the finite
empirical distribution; it is not the fair-ensemble estimator. Euclidean
norms are not divided by $K$. The variogram score uses $p=1/2$ and equal
weights over distinct unordered coordinates:
\begin{equation}
 \widehat{\mathrm{VS}}_{p} = \binom K2^{-1}
 \sum_{i<j}\left(|y_i-y_j|^p-
       \frac1S\sum_s|x_i^{(s)}-x_j^{(s)}|^p\right)^2,
 \qquad K\geq2.
\end{equation}
The score is undefined at $K=1$. Scores are not compared across dimensions
or normalizations as if they shared one scale. Variogram scores are not
strictly proper over unrestricted joint distributions and cannot detect
all defects; they complement rather than replace other diagnostics.

To construct a controlled dependence defect, choose a separate permutation
$\pi_k$ of $\{1,\ldots,S\}$ for each flattened coordinate $k$ and set
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde{x}^{(s)}_k=x^{(\pi_k(s))}_k.
 \label{eq:permutation}
\end{equation}
\paragraph{Proposition (empirical marginal invariance).}
For any ensemble and coordinate permutations in
Equation~\eqref{eq:permutation}, each empirical marginal distribution is
unchanged. Consequently, every deterministic statistic or score depending
only on these marginals and the observation is unchanged. This includes
coordinate means, empirical marginal quantiles, and average marginal CRPS.

\paragraph{Proof.}
For each coordinate $k$, reindexing the finite sum gives
$S^{-1}\sum_s\delta_{\widetilde{x}^{(s)}_k}
=S^{-1}\sum_s\delta_{x^{(s)}_k}$, where $\delta_z$ is a point mass at $z$.
Any function of these empirical marginal measures therefore has the same
value before and after permutation. Numerical implementations may differ
by floating-point rounding.\hfill$\square$

Joint trajectory pairing generally changes. Independent random
permutations tend to disrupt the dependence in a correlated ensemble,
although a finite permutation need not eliminate it entirely. This simple
identity supplies an executable negative control for marginal diagnostics,
rather than a new distributional result. It does not imply that every
permutation increases every joint score for each realized future. If the
reference itself factorizes across coordinates, independent permutations
do not create the same population dependence defect.

\section{Controlled evaluation protocol}

\subsection{Questions and experimental units}

The pilot (Study 1 in the experiments guide) uses 64 evaluation seeds
(10000--10063), disjoint from
development seeds 0--15. Its joint-sample task has a context of 120
observations, $H=8$, $D=2$, and $S=128$. The AR(1) coefficient is 0.8
and the innovation correlation is 0.7. The executable configuration and
generated results record any changed settings.

The pilot asks whether the implemented checks detect selected output and
semantic corruptions; whether removing a known corruption restores the
affected checks without worsening the tested clean behavior; and whether
joint evaluation responds when marginal sample distributions are
preserved. The unit of replication is an independently generated
scenario-seed case. Multiple horizons and targets within one case are
not treated as independent replications. Each case fixes one forecast
origin and refits the pipeline, a fixed-origin design with recalibration
in Tashman's terms; for a single real series, rolling origins over
multiple test periods are more efficient~\cite{tashman2000out}, and
ordinary $K$-fold cross-validation is valid for purely autoregressive
models with uncorrelated errors~\cite{bergmeir2018note}. Independent
synthetic cases replace neither procedure.

For each selected mutation, the clean, faulty, and repaired variants use
the same generated case. Structural checks provide a baseline for
malformed outputs. A conventional realized-loss threshold, calibrated
on separate clean cases when used, supplies a second comparison. A
reported advantage over that threshold applies only to the specified
calibration and test distribution, not to every possible holdout test.
We do not report a head-to-head comparison with sktime conformance tests
or the recent synthetic benchmarks.

\subsection{Controls, selection, and repair}

The unmodified last-value, seasonal-naive (period 12), and fitted Gaussian
AR(1) baselines illustrate capability limitations without intentionally
inserted software defects. Privileged reference
outputs test the mechanics of evaluation and are not counted as learned
forecasting achievements. Faulty outputs are created with one known
corruption at a time. Repair means removing that specified corruption and
rechecking the same contracts; there is no automated repair discovery.

Calibration cases and evaluation seeds are disjoint. Held-out seeds
provide new stochastic draws, not held-out mechanisms. Mutations are
selected to illustrate the implemented diagnostic classes, which favors
detectability. Consequently, detection rates quantify this selected
corpus, not the frequency or detectability of naturally occurring faults.
Mutation analysis rests on the coupling of simple seeded faults to real
ones~\cite{jia2011analysis}. Generated mutants have been found similar
in detectability to real faults, whereas hand-seeded faults were harder
to detect~\cite{andrews2005mutation}; in a corpus of 357 real faults, 73\%
were coupled to common mutants and 17\% to none~\cite{just2014mutants}.
The present corpus is hand-selected and therefore closer to the
hand-seeded case. In deep learning, mutation operators have instead been
derived from a taxonomy of real
faults~\cite{humbatova2020taxonomy,humbatova2021deepcrime}, and mutant
killing is defined statistically because retraining alone moves
accuracy~\cite{jahangirova2020empirical}; no comparable taxonomy of
forecasting-pipeline faults informs the present selection, and the
calibrated loss alarm of Section~\ref{sec:implementation-study} plays the
corresponding statistical role here.
Reports retain misses, unsupported cases, exceptions, and clean false
alarms. Statistical uncertainty is computed over independent cases, as
recommended for randomized procedures~\cite{arcuri2011practical}, and
the protocol records its exact convention with the results.

Six output corruptions displace the forecast index, swap target labels,
truncate the horizon, insert a nonfinite point, cross quantiles, or
transpose the sample axes. These are intentionally direct contract
violations; their detection tests the implementation of the contract
rather than demonstrating discovery of subtle bugs. Two further
mutations shrink ensemble variation or permute trajectory coordinates.
They retain well-formed outputs and exercise the reference-covariance
check. A separate preprocessing example omits inverse scaling in a
standardized historical-mean predictor and rechecks a declared
shift-equivariance relation after restoring that step.

The sample-dependence experiment begins with correct conditional paths,
applies Equation~\eqref{eq:permutation}, and compares the resulting
paired marginal and joint scores. Clean and corrupted paths share the
same empirical marginals by construction. The question is the response
of the evaluation measures to the known mutation, rather than the
relative performance of learned probabilistic models.

\subsection{Implementation regressions and calibrated loss alarms}
\label{sec:implementation-study}

The supplement (Study 2), a separately recorded protocol, moves the
injected faults inside a fitted forecasting pipeline. A separate six-lag recursive lag-Ridge predictor
uses an unpenalized intercept, penalty 1, and standardized targets.
Four branches reverse the prediction-time lag order, retain stale
recursive state, omit inverse target scaling, or silently swap the two
numeric target columns while preserving their labels. Each changes an
implementation operation and returns a well-shaped forecast. The repair
refits the corrected implementation on the identical context.

Six fixed conditions cover white noise with unequal target locations,
positive and negative AR(1), opposing trends, seasonality, and random
walks with drift. Every condition has 64 evaluation cases and 128 separate
clean calibration cases. These expand the parameter settings, but the
faults and mechanisms remain developer-selected. The full parameters,
seed ranges, transformations, and tolerances are stored in the second
protocol before its evaluation run.

Five comparators ask different questions: the output contract; scalar
shift equivariance with shift 10; per-target shift equivariance with
shifts $(7,-11)$; agreement with an independently implemented NumPy
lag-Ridge reference; and a calibrated realized-MSE alarm. The scalar
relation uses the public diagnostic. Per-target shifts and implementation
agreement are experimental comparators. The NumPy reference independently
constructs lag columns and solves augmented normal equations with an
unpenalized intercept in the original target units. It receives neither
the future nor generator parameters and checks algorithm agreement, not
forecast optimality. Numerical comparisons use fixed absolute tolerance
$10^{-8}$ and relative tolerance $10^{-7}$.

For each condition let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n$, $n=128$, be realized MSEs
from clean calibration cases and let $\ell$ be the evaluation-case MSE.
The split-calibration rank rule is
\begin{equation}
 p_{\mathrm{loss}}=\frac{1+\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}\{\ell_i\geq\ell\}}{n+1},
 \qquad \text{alarm if }p_{\mathrm{loss}}\leq0.05.
 \label{eq:loss-rank}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, reject above calibration order statistic
$\lceil(n+1)(1-0.05)\rceil$, with conservative ties. For a fixed clean
algorithm under the same case-generating condition, calibration and test
losses are exchangeable, yielding a marginal finite-sample rejection
bound by the split-conformal rank argument~\cite{lei2018conformal}.
This probability averages over calibration and test samples. It does not
guarantee a 5\% rejection probability conditional on the one calibration
sample actually drawn. The reported Wilson intervals condition on that
frozen calibration sample; no common threshold is pooled across conditions.

Each faulty case is paired with its clean and repaired runs. We retain
new alarms, lost alarms, misses, and repaired-minus-faulty losses, rather
than interpreting an unpaired fault alarm rate as diagnostic improvement.
Loss intervals use case-level paired differences within a condition.
Restoring agreement with the clean algorithm need not improve realized
loss on every noisy future.

\subsection{Covariance conditions and multiplicity}

The supplement also evaluates 64 independent four-task suites. Each
suite contains factorized white noise, correlated white noise, negative
AR(1), and a correlated random walk with drift, with $H=6$, $D=2$, $S=64$, and
$B=199$ null ensembles per check. Clean reference samples are paired with
a partial coordinate shuffle and with a 0.75 multiplier on deviations
from the conditional mean. The shuffle permutes half the sample indices
within each coordinate while preserving its complete empirical marginal.

For each variant, the four condition-specific tests form one declared
family. We report individual rejections, any raw rejection in a suite,
and any rejection after Holm's step-down adjustment~\cite{holm1979multiple}.
With sorted valid null $p$-values, Holm compares the $j$th value against
$0.05/(4-j+1)$ and stops at the first non-rejection. Its family-wise
guarantee concerns this fixed family; it does not extend to comparisons
across variants, study sections, or adaptive revisions of the protocol.
The factorized white-noise shuffle is a negative control: independent
coordinates remain independent under these sample permutations, so a
rejection is a false alarm rather than successful defect detection.

\subsection{Selected fault detection and false alarms}

Table~\ref{tab:faults} reports alarms for each selected corruption. The six explicit output violations were detected in every evaluation case. Both well-formed ensemble mutations were rejected by the covariance check in every case. These counts describe deliberately selected fixtures; they are not an estimate of detection across naturally occurring bugs.

Clean control & 5/64 [3.4, 17.0] & 0/64 [0.0, 5.7] & 6/64 [4.4, 19.0] \\

Index shift & 5/64 [3.4, 17.0] & 64/64 [94.3, 100.0] & --- \\

Target-label swap & 5/64 [3.4, 17.0] & 64/64 [94.3, 100.0] & --- \\

The clean covariance check rejected 6/64 cases (9.4\%; Wilson interval [4.4, 19.0]\%). The observed rate is above the nominal 5\% per-check level, with an interval that includes 5\%. No threshold was changed to remove these false alarms. The selected run does not establish precise calibration or a family-wise error rate.

The point-MSE cutoff was 4.1853, the empirical 95th percentile from 16 development cases. It alarmed on 5/64 clean cases. It detects invalid point arrays, but ignores index labels, target names, quantiles, and trajectory samples. Where a mutation leaves the point values unchanged, its alarms are identical to the clean alarms and supply no mutation-specific evidence.

Disabling an output mutation restored the exact clean output, including its sample array. Repaired outputs had zero contract violations and the same 6/64 covariance alarms as the clean control. These paired rechecks confirm removal of the selected corruption; they do not imply that every repaired case receives a statistical pass or that the framework discovered the repair.

\subsection{An implemented inverse-scaling repair}

A separate predictor standardizes its training context and forecasts the mean in standardized units. The fault omits the inverse transform; the repair applies the training mean and scale. The historical-mean predictor is shift equivariant, so this particular metamorphic relation is a valid declared contract. On white-noise cases with mean 5 and innovation scale 2, the relation failed for 64/64 faulty fits (Wilson 95\% interval [94.3, 100.0]\%) and 0/64 repaired fits ([0.0, 5.7]\%). The paired repaired-minus-faulty MAE difference was -3.4711 [-3.6333, -3.3090] (95\% t interval).

We then apply the same known omission and repair to AirPassengers, the monthly 1949--1960 international-airline passenger series in thousands~\cite{rAirPassengers}. All scaling statistics are fitted on each training prefix. The four ordered origins each forecast the next 12 months; their results are reported separately because they are not independent series replicates.

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small

\caption{AirPassengers inverse-scaling illustration. MAE is in thousands of passengers. The declared shift relation fails before and passes after repair at all four origins.}

\label{tab:real}

\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}\toprule

Last training month & Faulty MAE & Repaired MAE & Difference \\ \midrule

1956-12 & 368.42 & 154.71 & -213.71 \\

1957-12 & 381.00 & 150.10 & -230.90 \\

1958-12 & 428.33 & 182.43 & -245.91 \\

1959-12 & 476.17 & 213.67 & -262.49 \\

\bottomrule\end{tabular}\end{table}

Repair improves MAE at every displayed origin, but the repaired historical mean remains a poor model of this growing seasonal series. This is one known preprocessing defect on one dataset. It does not establish that synthetic diagnosis generally transfers to real forecasting tasks.

\subsection{Negative controls and multiple covariance checks}

The supplement's covariance study evaluates 64 independent suites, each containing four conditional-reference covariance checks with 64 predictive trajectories, 199 calibration ensembles, and nominal level 0.05. The fixed variants are exact-reference samples, partial dependence permutation (strength 0.5), and spread multiplied by 0.75. Raw and Holm decisions are reported for the declared four-check families. Shuffled factorized white noise remains a negative control.

For clean suites, any false alarm occurred in 14/64 raw suites versus 3/64 after Holm correction. For reduced-spread suites, detection of at least one altered condition fell from 63/64 to 30/64. The correction thus reduces family-wise false alarms at a substantial power cost in this setting.

The retained study design requires 8,448 sklearn fits, 384 independent NumPy solves, and 768 covariance checks containing 152,832 calibration ensembles. % END GENERATED SUPPLEMENT

\subsection{What the checks establish}

The implementation ablation (Table~\ref{tab:supplement-ablation}) makes
the diagnostic distinction concrete. Reversing lags and retaining stale
state preserve both translation relations even though they disagree with
the intended algorithm. A common shift also misses a numeric target swap;
different target shifts expose it. These outcomes follow the properties
being tested, rather than a universal ordering of diagnostic quality.
Independent implementation agreement is more discriminating in this
corpus, but requires a second specification of the intended algorithm
and does not establish forecasting optimality.

The repair counterexample further separates verification from model
selection. Correcting the stale-state regression restores the declared
recursive algorithm, while the random-walk condition with drift favors the faulty
variant's realized loss. A score can therefore reward a specification
violation, just as a conforming model can forecast poorly. A useful report
retains both observations rather than relabeling one as the other.

For probabilistic forecasts, marginal-preserving permutations isolate a
blind spot without relying on a noisy difference in marginal quality.
The factorized negative control is equally important: shuffling samples
is not itself evidence of a fault when the intended law has independent
coordinates. The covariance results (Tables~\ref{tab:supplement-familywise}
and~\ref{tab:supplement-covariance}) also show why per-check rejection and
suite-level false alarms must be reported separately, together with the
power lost after multiplicity adjustment.

\section{Limitations and implications}

The evidence concerns specified properties under controlled conditions.
The controlled fault-study corpus remains Gaussian and developer-selected.
The broader software catalog adds multivariate financial mechanisms and
compositions, but those additions have not been evaluated in an independent
real-bug corpus. Known DGP parameters and declared change schedules make
references more informative than those available to an ordinary fitted
forecaster; jump-regime filtering is approximate and cannot calibrate the
exact covariance rank check. CCC-GARCH cross-covariance integration has
Monte Carlo error, explicitly separate from its exact conditional simulator.
The joint extensions implement shared jump clocks and shared hidden chains,
not arbitrary idiosyncratic-jump, cross-lag, or dynamic-correlation systems.
A reference discrepancy can
therefore reflect estimation or model limitations. Marginal invariance
under coordinate permutations is an exact algebraic property; the power
of a particular joint check remains an empirical question.

All faults are selected and visible to the developer, and all repairs
are specified in advance. The implementation supplement moves beyond
output corruption but does not supply an independent corpus of naturally
occurring defects. The mathematical comparator verifies one intended
algorithm; it cannot establish that the algorithm is appropriate for
every forecasting task. These studies assess detection and repair
rechecks, not automatic source-code localization or repair discovery.

Statistical guarantees apply to their stated nulls and sampling units.
The covariance rank check (Equation~\eqref{eq:mc}) assumes independent
reference-law samples; the loss rank check (Equation~\eqref{eq:loss-rank})
assumes exchangeable clean cases within a condition.
Numerical conformance tolerances are engineering choices. Holm adjustment
protects only the declared four-check family. Other reported comparisons
are descriptive, and fresh evaluation seeds do not undo adaptive choice
of scenarios, mutations, or diagnostics.

AirPassengers supplies one known preprocessing repair at four origins
from one real series (Table~\ref{tab:real}). It does not establish synthetic-to-real transfer.
The scenario families were chosen for transparent references, not for
representativeness; even forecasting benchmark collections differ from
the distribution of real series~\cite{spiliotis2020forecasting}.
A broader study should prospectively collect faults from independent
repositories, compare directly with relevant framework tests, and
evaluate documented repairs on additional real tasks and unseen
mechanisms. Those results are needed to assess practical coverage and
external validity. The present artifact makes such a comparison possible
by retaining test specifications, paired cases, misses, and false alarms.

\section{Conclusion}

TimeGym connects forecast specifications to reproducible diagnostic
evidence. Its conditional references separate excess squared-error risk
from future noise, while typed outputs and declared relations distinguish
different kinds of failure. The selected implementation study shows that
valid outputs and translation equivariance can coexist with algorithmic
regressions, and that restoring an algorithm need not improve its forecast
loss. The probabilistic study makes the corresponding distinction between
marginal quality and joint dependence, including a null-preserving
negative control and explicit multiplicity handling. Together these
results support a practical discipline: state the property, reproduce the
case, inspect the evidence, and verify a proposed repair against both the
original failure and clean controls. The accompanying software and paired
records provide a basis for testing that discipline on independently
collected forecasting defects.

\paragraph{Software and reproducibility.}
The implementation and executable study accompany this manuscript in the
\href{https://github.com/diogoseca/timegym}{TimeGym repository}. See the
repository README for installation, test, and experiment commands. The
artifact is developed in executable source notebooks, exported to
package modules with nbdev. An explicit build checks complete module
ownership and detects notebook--module drift without executing examples.
Application notebooks cover univariate
and multivariate forecasts, marginal and joint uncertainty, fault diagnosis,
repair checks, replay, real-data integration, and capability sweeps. A
separate checker executes every active notebook in a fresh kernel; these teaching
examples are distinct from the two controlled studies reported here. The
generated result fragments record the run configurations, following the
reporting recommendations for forecasting research: a well-defined
data-generating process with its seeds, described methods and
parameterization, software versions, and defined
measures~\cite{makridakis2018objectivity}. Results correspond
to the pilot source digest \texttt{dece174f629b2647} and supplement result
digest \texttt{13b1228e7124b95f}, which was \texttt{ba9b2e90145ca50d} before
two offline record migrations that changed no value; their complete SHA-256
values are recorded in the respective experiment manifests.
